strengths: Compelling extension of mechanistic interpretability: The paper successfully extends causal mediation analysis and the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) from unimodal LLMs to multimodal relational reasoning in LMMs, addressing a prominent challenge in vision-language systems.

Methodological breadth and compositionality: The proposed composite function vector (CFV) approach for one-shot analogy tasks provides an elegant, principled way to evaluate linear compositional representations for unseen relations (e.g., combining base spatial vectors to represent 'above-left').

Thorough experimental validation: The study evaluates both synthetic controlled environments and natural images (GQA) across two distinct relation domains (spatial and agentic). The inclusion of out-of-distribution object evaluations and cross-dataset transfer (Synthetic to GQA) demonstrates robust generalization.

Detailed ablation and circuit analysis: The paper includes extensive analyses exploring layer depth sensitivity, attention head sparsity (showing peak performance with 6-12 heads), in-context prompt lengths, and cross-model representational similarity analysis (RSA).
weaknesses: Lack of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines: The fine-tuning experiment optimizes a single continuous vector added to layer hidden states over 1,000–2,000 examples. While comparing against 4-shot ICL demonstrates fast adaptation, comparing against standard parameter-matched parameter-efficient baselines (such as prefix tuning, soft prompt tuning, or low-rank adaptation on the same training split) would clarify whether the performance boost is specifically attributable to the function vector formulation or general continuous representation optimization.

Limited variety of modern LMM architectures: The evaluation is conducted on OpenFlamingo-4B (an older cross-attention model with low baseline accuracy) and Qwen-VL (4B). Evaluating an additional contemporary unified architecture family (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT or InternVL) would strengthen the universality of the mechanistic findings.

Terminology/citation discrepancy: The manuscript repeatedly refers to 'Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct', but citations and public checkpoints point to the Qwen2.5-VL series and general technical preprints. Clarifying the exact checkpoint and ensuring consistent naming is important for reproducibility.

strengths: The paper successfully and rigorously extends the function vector (FV) and causal mediation framework from language-only models to Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), specifically addressing the challenging domain of visual relational reasoning (spatial and agentic).

Thorough experimental methodology spanning both synthetic images (with controlled configurations and held-out object sets) and naturalistic scenes (GQA Spatial and GQA Agentic), evaluated across two distinct architectures (OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL).

Compelling demonstration of compositional generalization: the one-shot analogy experiment nicely operationalizes the linear representation hypothesis by demonstrating that composite function vectors (CFVs) can be synthesized dynamically from source demonstrations to solve novel, untrained relation tasks (e.g., above-right).

Comprehensive analysis and ablations, including causal mediation heatmaps, layer-wise injection sensitivity, attention head subset size trade-offs, cross-dataset transfer (synthetic to GQA), and representational similarity analysis across model backbones.
weaknesses: Fine-tuning function vectors (FFV) essentially acts as a parameter-efficient steering or single-vector prefix/bias tuning method. While the comparison against few-shot ICL and initial FVs is informative, the paper lacks comparison against standard lightweight adaptation baselines (such as prompt tuning, prefix tuning, or soft prompt injection at intermediate layers) to isolate how much benefit comes specifically from initializing with causally identified attention head activations.

The evaluation relies strictly on top-1 exact match on the first generated token for target object identification. While this is standard in token-level probing, it may penalize valid synonyms or multi-token entity generations, especially in naturalistic GQA evaluations.

The scope of models is limited to two ~4B parameter models (OpenFlamingo-4B and Qwen3-VL-4B). Extending the causal intervention experiments to larger or differently aligned architectures (e.g., larger Qwen2.5-VL / LLaVA-NeXT variants) would further corroborate the universality of these visual relation circuits.

strengths: Principled extension of mechanistic interpretability to vision-language models: Extending the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) to visual relational reasoning (both spatial and agentic relations) addresses an important and under-explored challenge in multimodal model interpretability.

Methodologically sound causal analysis: The use of causal mediation analysis with carefully designed uninformative/perturbed control prompts (balancing relation types) provides convincing evidence that specific mid-layer attention heads causally mediate visual relation representations.

Thorough ablations: The manuscript systematically investigates key design variables, including injection layer depth, head set size (showing a clear sparsity peak at 6–12 heads), context prompt length, and cross-model representational similarity.

Compelling compositional analogy formulation: The proposed composite function vector (CFV) approach—inferring mixture weights from a source analogy to steer predictions on unseen composite relations—is an elegant and practical operationalization of the linear representation hypothesis in multimodal latent spaces.

Cross-dataset and cross-object evaluation: Testing on held-out object sets and demonstrating zero-shot transfer from synthetic-derived vectors to the naturalistic GQA dataset strengthens the claim that these vectors capture generalizable relational concepts rather than dataset-specific visual artifacts.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison for fine-tuned function vectors (FFVs): While the initial (untrained) function vectors are appropriately compared to 0-shot and few-shot ICL, fine-tuned function vectors (FFVs) are optimized over 1,000–2,000 examples with gradient descent. Comparing FFV performance solely against few-shot ICL without parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines (e.g., continuous soft prompt tuning, prefix tuning of equivalent dimensionality, or linear probing) makes it difficult to assess how much gain comes from the function vector representation versus standard supervised parameter optimization.

Evaluation metric and label ambiguity: Task accuracy is measured by whether the highest-ranked output token matches the first token of the target label. In natural images (such as GQA), an object pair may satisfy multiple valid spatial or functional descriptions, and multi-token object names can introduce evaluation artifacts. The manuscript does not clarify whether prediction was restricted to a closed candidate set or computed over the entire vocabulary, nor does it provide an error analysis of common failure modes.

Model specification and reproducibility details: The paper designates one model as 'Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct' (citing recent 2025 reports/checkpoints alongside Qwen2.5-VL citations). Clearer specification of the exact checkpoint release, architecture parameters, and Hugging Face identifier is necessary to ensure experimental reproducibility.

Heuristic weight formulation in composite vectors: Weighting base relations via uncalibrated model output probabilities P(y_1 | x_1, v_t) in Eq. 5 assumes uniform token prior probabilities across different relation injections, which may be susceptible to base-rate frequency biases or uneven head activation magnitudes across relations.

strengths: The extension of the function vector (FV) paradigm and causal mediation analysis from text-only LLMs to vision-language models for spatial relational reasoning is a natural and conceptual step forward for multimodal mechanistic interpretability.

The composite function vector (CFV) formulation for zero-shot analogy transfer to untrained compositional relations (e.g., combining cardinal directions into ordinal ones like above-left) is creative and aligns well with the linear representation hypothesis.
The paper provides insightful ablations regarding the impact of the injection layer, the number of top attention heads included in the function vector, and the context length during extraction.
weaknesses: Evaluations are limited strictly to a single model architecture, OpenFlamingo-4B. Modern multimodal LLMs predominantly adopt autoregressive unified-transformer architectures (e.g., LLaVA, Qwen-VL, PaliGemma) rather than interleaved cross-attention architectures. It remains unclear whether the localized causal heads and vector transferability hold in unified decoder-only LMMs.

The comparison in Section 3.3.4 / 4.3 between fine-tuned function vectors and in-context learning is not fully equitable. Fine-tuning optimizes a continuous vector parameter directly on 1,000 synthetic examples or 101 real images via gradient descent, whereas ICL is completely training-free. A proper baseline would include parameter-matched soft prompt tuning, visual prompt tuning, or prefix tuning to isolate whether the causal FV initialization provides advantages over random continuous vectors.

The scope of datasets is limited. The real-image dataset comprises only 201 curated images from GQA with very strict filtering rules, and the synthetic dataset uses an artificial 6-object layout. In addition, the absolute task accuracy remains quite low across several evaluations (e.g., 16.8% top-1 accuracy on composite analogy tasks in Figure 6, and under 30% for synthetic relations in Figure 5).

Several presentation and typographical flaws detract from polish, including section headings ('LARGE LANGUAGE MOELS' in Section 2.1), missing punctuation in caption 4, and typos such as 'approch' (p. 2), 'rans' (p. 4), 'lable' (p. 6), and 'analog' (p. 6).

strengths: Timely and conceptually interesting research direction: Extending mechanistic interpretability and function vectors (FVs) from text-only LLMs to vision-language models for relational reasoning is a worthwhile pursuit.

Principled causal mediation framework: The adaptation of Average Indirect Effect (AIE) to identify causally salient attention heads in an interleaved cross-attention architecture (OpenFlamingo) is clearly formulated and methodologically structured.

Novel concept of Composite Function Vectors (CFVs): Formulating one-shot analogy reasoning as a convex combination of elementary spatial relation vectors (weighted by posterior likelihood) is an elegant operationalization of the linear representation hypothesis.
Comprehensive ablation studies: The appendix provides informative analyses regarding injection depth, head set cardinality, and demonstration prompt length.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison for fine-tuned vectors: In Section 4.3 and Figure 5, the fine-tuned function vector is directly compared against 4-shot in-context learning. However, the fine-tuned FV is optimized using the Adam optimizer over 1,000 examples (synthetic) or 101 images across 20 epochs, whereas ICL has access to only 4 examples at inference time. To demonstrate that the fine-tuned FV is uniquely advantageous, the authors should compare it against standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines trained on the same data, such as soft prompt tuning or LoRA.

Evaluation on a single, dated architecture: All experiments are conducted exclusively on OpenFlamingo-4B (ViT-L/14 + RedPajama-3B with gated cross-attention). Modern open-source LMMs (e.g., LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen2-VL, PaliGemma) predominantly use direct visual token projection into decoder-only backbones without cross-attention blocks. It remains unproven whether the identified head localization and vector manipulation generalize to modern mainstream architectures.

Severely restricted dataset scale and ecological validity: The real-image evaluation is performed on an extremely small subset of GQA consisting of only 201 images (101 train, 100 test). Evaluating zero-shot generalization on merely 100 unique real-world images limits statistical power and raises questions regarding whether the extracted heads are generalizable or overfitted to this restricted set.

Low absolute performance and ambiguous chance levels: In Figure 6 (analogy task), the composite function vector achieves 16.8% top-1 accuracy. In the synthetic dataset where an image contains a query object and 5 other candidate objects (4 relational, 1 distractor), random selection among candidate objects in the scene yields 20% accuracy. The paper does not clarify whether the evaluation measures open-vocabulary generation over the full vocabulary or constrained prediction over candidate objects in the scene, leaving the true significance over chance level ambiguous.

Weak effect of raw (untrained) function vectors: In Figure 5(b), the initial (un-tuned) function vector extracted via causal mediation yields minimal improvement over the zero-shot baseline and barely matches or underperforms 4-shot ICL. This suggests that the zero-shot steering capability of raw multimodal FVs is weak prior to supervised gradient updates.

Presentation and proofreading oversights: The manuscript contains multiple typos and presentation flaws in prominent locations (e.g., 'MOELS' in Section 2.1 heading, 'approch' on page 2, 'illusation' and 'rans' on page 4, 'relation-secific' on page 5, 'lable' and 'target analog' on page 6, 'a synthetic images' on page 10, and a future access date 'June 10, 2025' in the Anthropic reference).

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: Extending mechanistic interpretability and the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) to multimodal models is an active and important research direction.

Interesting compositionality formulation: The composite function vector approach (Eq. 5-6), which computes weighted combinations of relation vectors based on source model likelihoods to tackle novel composite spatial relations (e.g., above-left), is intuitive and shows promising conceptual generalization.

Informative ablation studies: The paper provides useful empirical analyses regarding injection layer depth, head subset size, and prompt context length, demonstrating that causal effects are concentrated in intermediate layers and a sparse set of heads.
weaknesses: Limited architectural diversity: All experiments are conducted exclusively on OpenFlamingo-4B. OpenFlamingo relies on gated cross-attention layers interleaved into a frozen language model, which differs fundamentally from dominant modern multimodal architectures (such as LLaVA, Qwen-VL, or InternVL) that use direct visual-token projection into a unified decoder. It remains unclear whether the localized attention head behavior identified here generalizes to decoder-only multimodal models.

Unfair baseline comparison for fine-tuned function vectors: Section 4.3 demonstrates that fine-tuning function vectors with gradient descent on 1,000 synthetic examples (or 101 real images) outperforms zero-shot and 4-shot in-context learning. However, comparing gradient-optimized vectors against few-shot ICL is not an apples-to-apples comparison. To substantiate the claim that fine-tuning function vectors is uniquely beneficial, the authors should compare against standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) or prompt-tuning baselines (e.g., continuous soft prefix tuning or visual prompt tuning) trained on the same data budget.

Extremely restricted datasets and low absolute task performance: The real-image evaluation is restricted to a heavily curated subset of only 201 GQA images (101 train, 100 test), which limits confidence in real-world applicability. Furthermore, the overall top-1 accuracies across tasks remain low (e.g., ~15-30% in Figure 5 and 16.8% in Figure 6), raising questions about how reliably these representations steer the model's actual reasoning versus inducing token biases.

Presentation and proofreading flaws: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and formatting errors, including in major headers and captions (e.g., 'MOELS' in Section 2.1, 'approch' on page 2, 'Followng' on page 3, 'secific' and 'rans' on pages 4-5, 'lable' on page 6, and a mismatch between the text description in Section 4.1 mentioning 'above and left of' while the caption of Figure 4 lists 'above relation, right panel for right of relation').
